e-6106.knowledge_point: Evaluating a Double Integral Using the Multiplicative Property
e-6106.problem: Evaluate the double integral $\displaystyle \iint\limits_{R} xy\ \!e^{x+y}\ \textrm d A$ over the rectangle $R= [0,1] \times [1,2].$
e-6106.worked_solution:
We apply the multiplicative property of double integrals and then evaluate each of the integrals separately:

$$
\eqalign{
\iint\limits_{R}  xy\  e^{x+y}\: \textrm d A &= \iint\limits_{R} \Big( x\ \! e^x \Big)\Big( y\ \! e^{y} \Big) \textrm d A\[5pt]
&= \left(\int_0^1x\  e^{x}  \ \textrm d x\right)\left( \int_1^2 y \ \!e^{y} \ \textrm d y\right)\[5pt]
                                                                         &= \Big[x\ \!e^x-e^x\Big]_0^1 \cdot  \Big[y\ \!e^y-e^y\Big]_1^2\[5pt]
                                                                         &=  \Big(e^1-e^1 - \left(0-e^0\right)\Big) \cdot \Big(2e^2-e^2 - \left(e^1-e^1\right) \Big)\[5pt]
                                                                         &= 1\cdot e^2\[5pt]
                                                                         &= e^2
}
$$

e-6107.knowledge_point: Evaluating a Double Integral When the Integrand Contains Only One Variable
e-6107.worked_solution:
Using the linearity property of double integrals, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}+3)\text{ }\text{d}A & ={∬}_{R}{x}^{2}\text{ }\text{d}A-{∬}_{R}{y}^{2}\text{ }\text{d}A+{∬}_{R}3\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's evaluate each of the three integrals.

- The function under the first integral is independent of $y.$ So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}{x}^{2}\text{ }\text{d}A & =(4-2){\int }_{-1}^{3}{x}^{2}\text{ }\text{d}x \\  & =2\cdot \frac{{x}^{3}}{3}{|}_{-1}^{3} \\  & =2(\frac{27}{3}+\frac{1}{3}) \\  & =\frac{56}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

- The function under the second integral is independent of $x.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}{y}^{2}\text{ }\text{d}A & =(3-(-1)){\int }_{2}^{4}{y}^{2}\text{ }\text{d}y \\  & =4{\int }_{2}^{4}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =4\cdot \frac{{y}^{3}}{3}{|}_{2}^{4} \\  & =\frac{4}{3}{4}^{3}-\frac{4}{3}{2}^{3} \\  & =\frac{224}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

- The function under the third integral is a constant, so we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}3\,\text{d}A=3\,\text{Area}(R)=3\cdot (2\cdot 4)=24.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, combining our results, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}+3)\,\text{d}A=\frac{56}{3}-\frac{224}{3}+24=-32.\end{aligned}
$$

e-7023.problem:
Given that $C$ and $D$ are finite, non-overlapping regions and that

$$
\iint\limits_{C}  f(x,y)\ \textrm{d}A = 8,
\qquad
\iint\limits_{D}  f(x,y)\ \textrm{d}A = -5,
$$

find the value of 

$$
\iint\limits_{C \cup D}  3f(x,y)\ \textrm{d}A.
$$
e-7023.worked_solution:
Using the linearity and additivity of double integrals, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{C\cup D}3f(x,y)\text{ }\text{d}A & =3{∬}_{C\cup D}f(x,y)\text{ }\text{d}A \\  & =3({∬}_{C}f(x,y)\text{ }\text{d}A+{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }\text{d}A) \\  & =3(8+(-5)) \\  & =3\cdot 3 \\  & =9\end{aligned}
$$

e-6108.knowledge_point: Evaluating a Double Integral Using the Additivity Over a Rectangular Domain
e-6108.problem:
Evaluate the double integral $\displaystyle \iint\limits_{R}  f(x,y)\ \textrm d A$, where

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14099811/assets/feda4016e31449244cf758fe239e49c6dd384a91b216763f72210b3c1b213827.png)
and  $R$ is the domain of $f.$
e-6108.worked_solution:
First, notice that we have $R = R_1 \cup R_2,$ where $R_1= (0,2) \times (-1,0)$ and $R_2= (0,2) \times (0,1).$ So, we can write

$$
\eqalign{
\iint\limits_{R}  f(x,y)\ \textrm d A &= \iint\limits_{R_1} 2 \ \textrm d A + \iint\limits_{R_2}    \dfrac{1}{xy+x+y+1} \ \textrm d A\[5pt]
&= 2\iint\limits_{R_1} \textrm d A
+ \iint\limits_{R_2}  \dfrac{1}{(x+1)(y+1)} \ \textrm d A\[5pt]
&= 2(2-0)(0-(-1)) + \Bigg( \int_0^2 \dfrac{1}{x+1} \ \textrm d x \Bigg) \Bigg( \int_0^1 \dfrac{1}{y+1}\ \textrm d y \Bigg) \[5pt]
&= 4 + \Big[\ln(x+1)\Big]_0^2  \cdot \Big[\ln(y+1)\Big]_0^1\[5pt] 
&= 4+ \ln 3\ln 2.
}
$$

after.name: Question 1
after.problem: Evaluate the double integral ${∬}_{R}\frac{1}{xy}\,\text{d}A$ over the rectangle $R=[1,e]\times [e,{e}^{2}].$
after.worked_solution:
We apply the multiplicative property of double integrals and then evaluate each of the integrals separately:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}\frac{1}{xy}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{R}(\frac{1}{x})\text{ }(\frac{1}{y})\,\text{d}A \\  & =({\int }_{1}^{e}\frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x)({\int }_{e}^{{e}^{2}}\frac{1}{y}\,\text{d}y) \\  & =[\operatorname{ln}⁡x]_{1}^{e}\cdot [\operatorname{ln}⁡y]_{e}^{{e}^{2}} \\  & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡e-\operatorname{ln}⁡1)\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡{e}^{2}-\operatorname{ln}⁡e) \\  & =(1-0)\cdot (2-1) \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

before.html:
Question 2
?

Which of the following gives the value of the double integral ∬Rxycos⁡yxdA over the rectangle R=[1,2]×[0,π]?

a
 (∫0π1ydx)(∫12xcos⁡ydy)
b
 (∫12xydx)(∫0πcos⁡ydy)
c
 (∫12xdx)(∫0πycos⁡ydy)
d
 (∫121xdx)(∫0πycos⁡ydy)
e
 (∫0π1xdx)(∫12ycos⁡ydy)
Submit

decision.explanation: Since √(xy)/x = √y/√x on this rectangle, the multiplicative property separates the integral into (∫₁² 1/√x dx)(∫₀ᵖⁱ √y cos y dy), which is option d.

after.name: Question 2
after.problem: Which of the following gives the value of the double integral ${∬}_{R}\frac{\sqrt{xy}\operatorname{cos}⁡y}{x}\,\text{d}A$ over the rectangle $R=[1,2]\times [0,\pi ]?$
after.worked_solution:
We apply the multiplicative property of double integrals, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}\frac{\sqrt{xy}\operatorname{cos}⁡y}{x}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{R}\frac{1}{x}\,{x}^{1/2}\,{y}^{1/2}\,\operatorname{cos}⁡y\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{R}(\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}})\text{ }(\sqrt{y}\operatorname{cos}⁡y)\,\text{d}A \\  & =({\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}\,\text{d}x)({\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{y}\operatorname{cos}⁡y\,\text{d}y)\end{aligned}
$$

Question 2
?

Which of the following gives the value of the double integral ∬Rxycos⁡yxdA over the rectangle R=[1,2]×[0,π]?

a
 (∫0π1ydx)(∫12xcos⁡ydy)
b
 (∫12xydx)(∫0πcos⁡ydy)
c
 (∫12xdx)(∫0πycos⁡ydy)
d
 (∫121xdx)(∫0πycos⁡ydy)
e
 (∫0π1xdx)(∫12ycos⁡ydy)
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

We apply the multiplicative property of double integrals, as follows:

∬Rxycos⁡yxdA=∬R1xx1/2y1/2cos⁡ydA=∬R(1x) (ycos⁡y)dA=(∫121xdx)(∫0πycos⁡ydy)

verification.explanation: The revealed worked solution explicitly gives option d. This agrees with factoring the integrand as (1/√x)(√y cos y) and integrating each factor over its corresponding interval.

content.knowledge_point: Evaluating a Double Integral Using the Multiplicative Property
content.problem: Which of the following gives the value of the double integral ${∬}_{R}\frac{\sqrt{xy}\operatorname{cos}⁡y}{x}\,\text{d}A$ over the rectangle $R=[1,2]\times [0,\pi ]?$
content.worked_solution:
We apply the multiplicative property of double integrals, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}\frac{\sqrt{xy}\operatorname{cos}⁡y}{x}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{R}\frac{1}{x}\,{x}^{1/2}\,{y}^{1/2}\,\operatorname{cos}⁡y\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{R}(\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}})\text{ }(\sqrt{y}\operatorname{cos}⁡y)\,\text{d}A \\  & =({\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}\,\text{d}x)({\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{y}\operatorname{cos}⁡y\,\text{d}y)\end{aligned}
$$

before.html:
Question 3
?

Which of the following gives the value of the double integral ∬Rxy 1ydA over the rectangle R=[0,5]×[3,7]?

a
(∫05xdx)(∫371ydy)
b
(∫05x3dx)(∫37y2ydy)
c
(∫051xdx)(∫37ydy)
d
(∫37xdx)(∫051ydy)
e
(∫05xxdx)(∫37ydy)
Submit

decision.explanation: The integrand factors as √(xy)/y = √x/√y. Over R = [0,5] × [3,7], the multiplicative property therefore gives (∫₀⁵ √x dx)(∫₃⁷ 1/√y dy), matching option a.

after.name: Question 3
after.problem: Which of the following gives the value of the double integral ${∬}_{R}\sqrt{xy}\text{ }\frac{1}{y}\,\text{d}A$ over the rectangle $R=[0,5]\times [3,7]?$
after.worked_solution:
We apply the multiplicative property of double integrals, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}\sqrt{xy}\text{ }\frac{1}{y}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{R}{x}^{1/2}\,{y}^{1/2}\,{y}^{-1}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{R}({x}^{1/2})\text{ }({y}^{-1/2})\,\text{d}A \\  & =({\int }_{0}^{5}\sqrt{x}\,\text{d}x)({\int }_{3}^{7}\frac{1}{\sqrt{y}}\,\text{d}y)\end{aligned}
$$

a
(∫05xdx)(∫371ydy)
b

(∫37xdx)(∫051ydy)
e

EXPLANATION

We apply the multiplicative property of double integrals, as follows:

content.knowledge_point: Evaluating a Double Integral Using the Multiplicative Property
content.problem: Which of the following gives the value of the double integral ${∬}_{R}\sqrt{xy}\text{ }\frac{1}{y}\,\text{d}A$ over the rectangle $R=[0,5]\times [3,7]?$
content.worked_solution:
We apply the multiplicative property of double integrals, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}\sqrt{xy}\text{ }\frac{1}{y}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{R}{x}^{1/2}\,{y}^{1/2}\,{y}^{-1}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{R}({x}^{1/2})\text{ }({y}^{-1/2})\,\text{d}A \\  & =({\int }_{0}^{5}\sqrt{x}\,\text{d}x)({\int }_{3}^{7}\frac{1}{\sqrt{y}}\,\text{d}y)\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 4
after.problem: Evaluate the double integral ${∬}_{R}\frac{1}{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡y\,\text{d}A$ over the rectangle $R=[1,e]\times [0,\frac{\pi }{2}].$
after.worked_solution:
We apply the multiplicative property of double integrals and then evaluate each of the integrals separately:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}\frac{1}{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡y\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{R}(\frac{1}{x})(\operatorname{cos}⁡y)\,\text{d}A \\  & =({\int }_{1}^{e}\frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x)({\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡y\,\text{d}y) \\  & =[\operatorname{ln}⁡x]_{1}^{e}\cdot [\operatorname{sin}⁡y]_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡e-\operatorname{ln}⁡1)\cdot (\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-\operatorname{sin}⁡0) \\  & =(1-0)\cdot (1-0) \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

content.knowledge_point: Evaluating a Double Integral Using the Multiplicative Property
content.problem: Evaluate the double integral ${∬}_{R}\frac{1}{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡y\,\text{d}A$ over the rectangle $R=[1,e]\times [0,\frac{\pi }{2}].$
content.worked_solution:
We apply the multiplicative property of double integrals and then evaluate each of the integrals separately:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}\frac{1}{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡y\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{R}(\frac{1}{x})(\operatorname{cos}⁡y)\,\text{d}A \\  & =({\int }_{1}^{e}\frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x)({\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡y\,\text{d}y) \\  & =[\operatorname{ln}⁡x]_{1}^{e}\cdot [\operatorname{sin}⁡y]_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡e-\operatorname{ln}⁡1)\cdot (\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-\operatorname{sin}⁡0) \\  & =(1-0)\cdot (1-0) \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

before.html:
Question 5
?

Which of the following gives the value of the double integral ∬Ryx23x+y dA over the rectangle R=[1,3]×[0,2]?

a
(∫13yx2dx)(∫023x+ydy)
b
(∫13x2dx)(∫02y3x+ydy)
c
(∫02x23xdx)(∫13y3ydy)
d
(∫13x23xdx)(∫02y3ydy)
e
(∫02ydx)(∫13x23x+ydy)
Submit

decision.explanation: Since 3^(x+y) = 3^x·3^y, the integrand factors as (x²3^x)(y3^y). The multiplicative property over [1,3] × [0,2] gives exactly option d.

after.name: Question 5
after.problem: Which of the following gives the value of the double integral ${∬}_{R}y{x}^{2}{3}^{x+y}\text{ }\text{d}A$ over the rectangle $R=[1,3]\times [0,2]?$
after.worked_solution:
We apply the multiplicative property of double integrals, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}y{x}^{2}{3}^{x+y}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{R}y\,{x}^{2}\,{3}^{x}\,{3}^{y}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{R}({x}^{2}\,{3}^{x})\text{ }(y\,{3}^{y})\,\text{d}A \\  & =({\int }_{1}^{3}{x}^{2}\,{3}^{x}\,\text{d}x)({\int }_{0}^{2}y\,{3}^{y}\,\text{d}y)\end{aligned}
$$

content.knowledge_point: Evaluating a Double Integral Using the Multiplicative Property
content.problem: Which of the following gives the value of the double integral ${∬}_{R}y{x}^{2}{3}^{x+y}\text{ }\text{d}A$ over the rectangle $R=[1,3]\times [0,2]?$
content.worked_solution:
We apply the multiplicative property of double integrals, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}y{x}^{2}{3}^{x+y}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{R}y\,{x}^{2}\,{3}^{x}\,{3}^{y}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{R}({x}^{2}\,{3}^{x})\text{ }(y\,{3}^{y})\,\text{d}A \\  & =({\int }_{1}^{3}{x}^{2}\,{3}^{x}\,\text{d}x)({\int }_{0}^{2}y\,{3}^{y}\,\text{d}y)\end{aligned}
$$

a
 16
b
 18
c

d

e

Submit

decision.explanation: By linearity, the integral is 2∫₋₁⁰ 3x² dx + 1∫₀² 6y² dy = 2[x³]₋₁⁰ + [2y³]₀² = 2 + 16 = 18.

after.name: Question 6
after.worked_solution:
Using the linearity property of double integrals, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}(3{x}^{2}+6{y}^{2})\text{d}A & ={∬}_{R}3{x}^{2}\text{ }\text{d}A+{∬}_{R}6{y}^{2}\text{ }\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

The function under the first integral is independent of $y.$ So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}3{x}^{2}\text{ }\text{d}A & =(2-0){\int }_{-1}^{0}3{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2({x}^{3}{|}_{-1}^{0}) \\  & =2({0}^{3}-(-1)^{3}) \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

The function under the second integral is independent of $x.$ So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}6{y}^{2}\text{ }\text{d}A & =(0-(-1)){\int }_{0}^{2}6{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2{y}^{3}{|}_{0}^{2} \\  & =2\cdot {2}^{3}-0 \\  & =16.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, combining our results, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}(3{x}^{2}+6{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A=2+16=18.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}3{x}^{2}\text{ }\text{d}A & =(2-0){\int }_{-1}^{0}3{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2({x}^{3}{|}_{-1}^{0}) \\  & =2({0}^{3}-(-1)^{3}) \\  & =2.\end{aligned}

$$

Finally, combining our results, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}(3{x}^{2}+6{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A=2+16=18.\end{aligned}
$$

after.problem: Evaluate the double integral ${∬}_{R}\frac{1+y{x}^{3}}{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}A$,  where $R=[1,2]\times [0,8].$
after.worked_solution:
Using the linearity property of double integrals, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}\frac{1+y{x}^{3}}{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{R}(\frac{1}{{x}^{3}}+y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{R}\frac{1}{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{R}y\text{ }\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

The function under the first integral is independent of $y.$ So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}\frac{1}{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}A & =(8-0){\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =8\cdot (-\frac{1}{2{x}^{2}}{|}_{1}^{2}) \\  & =8\cdot (-\frac{1}{8}-(-\frac{1}{2})) \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

The function under the second integral is independent of $x.$ So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}y\text{ }\text{d}A & =(2-1){\int }_{0}^{8}y\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}{|}_{0}^{8} \\  & =\frac{{8}^{2}}{2}-\frac{{0}^{2}}{2} \\  & =32.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, combining our results, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}\frac{1+y{x}^{3}}{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}A=3+32=35.\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 8
after.problem: Evaluate the double integral ${∬}_{R}\frac{1+x\operatorname{sin}⁡y}{x}\,\text{d}A$,  where $R=[1,e]\times [0,\pi ].$
after.worked_solution:
Using the linearity property of double integrals, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}\frac{1+x\operatorname{sin}⁡y}{x}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{R}(\frac{1}{x}+\operatorname{sin}⁡y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{R}\frac{1}{x}\text{ }\text{d}A+{∬}_{R}\operatorname{sin}⁡y\text{ }\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

The function under the first integral is independent of $y.$ So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}\frac{1}{x}\text{ }\text{d}A & =(\pi -0){\int }_{1}^{e}\frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi \cdot [\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|]_{1}^{e} \\  & =\pi (\operatorname{ln}⁡e-\operatorname{ln}⁡1) \\  & =\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

The function under the second integral is independent of $x.$ So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}\operatorname{sin}⁡y\text{ }\text{d}A & =(e-1){\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,\text{d}y \\  & =(e-1)[-\operatorname{cos}⁡y]_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =(e-1)(-\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi +\operatorname{cos}⁡0) \\  & =2(e-1).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, combining our results, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}\frac{1+x\operatorname{sin}⁡y}{x}\,\text{d}A=\pi +2(e-1)=2e+\pi -2.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 8

Evaluate the double integral ∬R1+xsin⁡yxdA, where R=[1,e]×[0,π].

a
 2e+π
b
 π−e+1
c
 π+e
d
 2e−π+2
e
 2e+π−2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Using the linearity property of double integrals, we get

∬R1+xsin⁡yxdA=∬R(1x+sin⁡y)dA=∬R1x dA+∬Rsin⁡y dA.

The function under the first integral is independent of y. So, we have

∬R1x dA=(π−0)∫1e1xdx=π⋅[ln⁡|x|]1e=π(ln⁡e−ln⁡1)=π.

The function under the second integral is independent of x. So, we have

∬Rsin⁡y dA=(e−1)∫0πsin⁡ydy=(e−1)[−cos⁡y]0π=(e−1)(−cos⁡π+cos⁡0)=2(e−1).

Finally, combining our results, we obtain

∬R1+xsin⁡yxdA=π+2(e−1)=2e+π−2.

content.knowledge_point: Evaluating a Double Integral When the Integrand Contains Only One Variable
content.problem: Evaluate the double integral ${∬}_{R}\frac{1+x\operatorname{sin}⁡y}{x}\,\text{d}A$,  where $R=[1,e]\times [0,\pi ].$
content.worked_solution:
Using the linearity property of double integrals, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}\frac{1+x\operatorname{sin}⁡y}{x}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{R}(\frac{1}{x}+\operatorname{sin}⁡y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{R}\frac{1}{x}\text{ }\text{d}A+{∬}_{R}\operatorname{sin}⁡y\text{ }\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

The function under the first integral is independent of $y.$ So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}\frac{1}{x}\text{ }\text{d}A & =(\pi -0){\int }_{1}^{e}\frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi \cdot [\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|]_{1}^{e} \\  & =\pi (\operatorname{ln}⁡e-\operatorname{ln}⁡1) \\  & =\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

The function under the second integral is independent of $x.$ So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}\operatorname{sin}⁡y\text{ }\text{d}A & =(e-1){\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,\text{d}y \\  & =(e-1)[-\operatorname{cos}⁡y]_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =(e-1)(-\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi +\operatorname{cos}⁡0) \\  & =2(e-1).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, combining our results, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}\frac{1+x\operatorname{sin}⁡y}{x}\,\text{d}A=\pi +2(e-1)=2e+\pi -2.\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 9
after.problem: Calculate ${∬}_{R}({x}^{2}-y+1)\,\text{d}A$,  where $R=[-3,0]\times [0,4].$
after.worked_solution:
Using the linearity property of double integrals, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}({x}^{2}-y+1)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{R}{x}^{2}\text{ }\text{d}A-{∬}_{R}y\text{ }\text{d}A+{∬}_{R}\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

The function under the first integral is independent of $y.$ So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}{x}^{2}\text{ }\text{d}A & =(4-0){\int }_{-3}^{0}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =4[\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}]_{-3}^{0} \\  & =4(\frac{{0}^{3}}{3}-\frac{(-3)^{3}}{3}) \\  & =36.\end{aligned}
$$

The function under the second integral is independent of $x.$ So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}y\text{ }\text{d}A & =(0-(-3)){\int }_{0}^{4}y\,\text{d}y \\  & =3[\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}]_{0}^{4} \\  & =3(\frac{{4}^{2}}{2}-\frac{{0}^{2}}{2}) \\  & =24.\end{aligned}
$$

The third integral is the double integral of unity:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}\text{d}A=\text{Area}(R)=3\cdot 4=12\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, combining our results, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}({x}^{2}-y+1)\,\text{d}A=36-24+12=24.\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 10
after.problem: Calculate ${∬}_{R}(2+2x-3{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A$,  where $R=[0,3]\times [0,2].$
after.worked_solution:
Using the linearity property of double integrals, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}(2+2x-3{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{R}2\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{R}2x\,\text{d}A-{∬}_{R}3{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

The function under the first integral is a constant, so we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}2\,\text{d}A=2\,\text{Area}(R)=2\cdot (3\cdot 2)=12.\end{aligned}
$$

 

The function under the second integral is independent of $y.$ So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}2x\,\text{d}A & =(2-0){\int }_{0}^{3}2x\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\cdot [{x}^{2}]_{0}^{3} \\  & =2({3}^{2}-(0)^{2}) \\  & =18.\end{aligned}
$$

The function under the third integral is independent of $x.$ So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}2y\,\text{d}A & =(3-0){\int }_{0}^{2}3{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =3\cdot [{y}^{3}]_{0}^{2} \\  & =3({2}^{3}-{0}^{3}) \\  & =24.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, combining our results, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}(2+2x-3{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A=12+18-24=6.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 12
?

Consider the region R shown above. Let the function f(x,y) be defined as f(x,y)={xy,(x,y)∈S,x2−xy3,(x,y)∈T,0,(x,y)∈U. Then, ∬Rf(x,y) dA=

a
 ∬S∪T(xy+x2−xy3)dA
b
 ∬S∪Txy(x2−xy3)dA
c
 ∬SxydA+∬T(x2−xy3)dA+∬UdA
d
 ∬SxydA+∬U(x2−xy3)dA
e
 ∬SxydA+∬T(x2−xy3)dA
Submit

decision.explanation: Additivity splits the integral over R into integrals over S, T, and U. Use x/y on S and x²−xy³ on T; the integral over U is zero because f=0 there. This gives option e.

Consider the region $R$ shown above. Let the function $f(x,y)$ be defined as

$$
f(x,y)={\begin{aligned}\frac{x}{y}, & (x,y)\in S, \\ {x}^{2}-x{y}^{3}, & (x,y)\in T, \\ 0, & (x,y)\in U.\end{aligned}
$$

Then,

$$
{∬}_{R}f(x,y)\text{ }\text{d}A=
$$
after.worked_solution:
First, notice that the domain $R$ can be represented as a union of three sub-domains, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}R & =S\cup T\cup U.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{S}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{T}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{U}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{S}\frac{x}{y}\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{T}({x}^{2}-x{y}^{3})\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{U}0\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{S}\frac{x}{y}\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{T}({x}^{2}-x{y}^{3})\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

a
 ∬Sycos⁡xdA+∬Uex+ydA
b
 ∬Sycos⁡xdA+∬Tex+ydA
c
 ∬Sycos⁡xdA+∬TdA+∬Uex+ydA

decision.explanation: By additivity, integrate y cos x over S and e^(x+y) over U. The contribution from T is zero because f=0 there. This matches option a.

Consider the region $R$ shown above. Let the function $f(x,y)$ be defined as

$$
f(x,y)={\begin{aligned}y\operatorname{cos}⁡x, & (x,y)\in S, \\ 0, & (x,y)\in T, \\ {e}^{x+y}, & (x,y)\in U.\end{aligned}
$$

Then,

$$
{∬}_{R}f(x,y)\text{ }\text{d}A=
$$
after.worked_solution:
First, notice that the domain $R$ can be represented as a union of three sub-domains, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}R & =S\cup T\cup U.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{S}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{T}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{U}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{S}y\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{T}0\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{U}{e}^{x+y}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{S}y\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{U}{e}^{x+y}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the region R shown above. Let the function f(x,y) be defined as f(x,y)={ycos⁡x,(x,y)∈S,0,(x,y)∈T,ex+y,(x,y)∈U. Then, ∬Rf(x,y) dA=

a
 ∬Sycos⁡xdA+∬Uex+ydA
b
 ∬Sycos⁡xdA+∬Tex+ydA
c
 ∬Sycos⁡xdA+∬TdA+∬Uex+ydA
d
 ∬Sex+ydA+∬Uycos⁡xdA
e
 ∬Sycos⁡xdA+∬Tex+ydA+∬UdA
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, notice that the domain R can be represented as a union of three sub-domains, as follows:

R=S∪T∪U.

So, we can write

∬Rf(x,y)dA=∬Sf(x,y)dA+∬Tf(x,y)dA+∬Uf(x,y)dA=∬Sycos⁡xdA+∬T0dA+∬Uex+ydA=∬Sycos⁡xdA+∬Uex+ydA.

verification.explanation: The revealed worked solution gives option a: integrate y cos x over S and e^(x+y) over U. The integral over T is zero, agreeing with the piecewise definition.

$$

decision.explanation: By additivity, integrate ∛x·y − ∛y over S and 2xy³ over T. The contribution from U is zero. This matches option d.

after.worked_solution:
First, notice that the domain $R$ can be represented as a union of three sub-domains, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}R & =S\cup T\cup U.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we can write

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

Consider the region R shown above. Let the function f(x,y) be defined as f(x,y)={xy,(x,y)∈S,0,(x,y)∈T,x2+y2,(x,y)∈U. Then, ∬Rf(x,y) dA=

a
 ∬S∪Uxy(x2+y2)dA
b
 ∬SxydA+∬U(x2+y2)dA
c
 ∬S∪U(xy+x2+y2)dA
d
 ∬SxydA+∬T(x2+y2)dA
e
 ∬SxydA+∬TdA+∬U(x2+y2)dA
Submit

decision.explanation: By additivity, integrate √(xy) over S and x²+y² over U. The contribution from T is zero because f=0 there. This matches option b.

Consider the region $R$ shown above. Let the function $f(x,y)$ be defined as

$$
f(x,y)={\begin{aligned}\sqrt{xy}, & (x,y)\in S, \\ 0, & (x,y)\in T, \\ {x}^{2}+{y}^{2}, & (x,y)\in U.\end{aligned}
$$

Then,

$$
{∬}_{R}f(x,y)\text{ }\text{d}A=
$$
after.worked_solution:
First, notice that the domain $R$ can be represented as a union of three sub-domains, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}R & =S\cup T\cup U.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{S}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{T}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{U}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{S}\sqrt{xy}\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{T}0\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{U}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{S}\sqrt{xy}\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{U}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the region R shown above. Let the function f(x,y) be defined as f(x,y)={xy,(x,y)∈S,0,(x,y)∈T,x2+y2,(x,y)∈U. Then, ∬Rf(x,y) dA=

a
 ∬S∪Uxy(x2+y2)dA
b
 ∬SxydA+∬U(x2+y2)dA
c
 ∬S∪U(xy+x2+y2)dA
d
 ∬SxydA+∬T(x2+y2)dA
e
 ∬SxydA+∬TdA+∬U(x2+y2)dA
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, notice that the domain R can be represented as a union of three sub-domains, as follows:

R=S∪T∪U.

So, we can write

∬Rf(x,y)dA=∬Sf(x,y)dA+∬Tf(x,y)dA+∬Uf(x,y)dA=∬SxydA+∬T0dA+∬U(x2+y2)dA=∬SxydA+∬U(x2+y2)dA.

content.worked_solution:
First, notice that the domain $R$ can be represented as a union of three sub-domains, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}R & =S\cup T\cup U.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{S}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{T}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{U}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{S}\sqrt{xy}\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{T}0\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{U}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{S}\sqrt{xy}\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{U}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

and  $R$ is the domain of $f.$

decision.explanation: Split the region at y=2 and integrate each formula over its defining rectangle. The missing line y=2 has area zero and does not affect the integral. This gives option c.

First, notice that the rectangle $R$ can be represented as a union of two smaller rectangles, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}R & =(1,2)\times ((1,2)\cup (2,4)) \\  & =((1,2)\times (1,2))\cup ((1,2)\times (2,4)).\end{aligned}
$$

So, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{(1,2)\times (1,2)}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{(1,2)\times (2,4)}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{(1,2)\times (1,2)}\frac{y+1}{1+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{(1,2)\times (2,4)}\frac{{x}^{2}}{{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$
content.worked_solution:
First, notice that the rectangle $R$ can be represented as a union of two smaller rectangles, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}R & =(1,2)\times ((1,2)\cup (2,4)) \\  & =((1,2)\times (1,2))\cup ((1,2)\times (2,4)).\end{aligned}
$$

So, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{(1,2)\times (1,2)}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{(1,2)\times (2,4)}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{(1,2)\times (1,2)}\frac{y+1}{1+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{(1,2)\times (2,4)}\frac{{x}^{2}}{{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

b

decision.explanation: Split the region at x=0. Integrate x²+y² over (−1,0)×(1,3) and 2√(xy) over (0,2)×(1,3), giving option d. The undefined line x=0 has area zero and does not affect the integral.

$$

$$
after.worked_solution:
First, notice that the rectangle $R$ can be represented as a union of two smaller rectangles, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}R & =((-1,0)\cup (0,2))\times (1,3) \\  & =((-1,0)\times (1,3))\cup ((0,2)\times (1,3)).\end{aligned}
$$

So, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{(-1,0)\times (1,3)}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{(0,2)\times (1,3)}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{(-1,0)\times (1,3)}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{(0,2)\times (1,3)}2\sqrt{xy}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

content.worked_solution:
First, notice that the rectangle $R$ can be represented as a union of two smaller rectangles, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}R & =((-1,0)\cup (0,2))\times (1,3) \\  & =((-1,0)\times (1,3))\cup ((0,2)\times (1,3)).\end{aligned}
$$

So, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{(-1,0)\times (1,3)}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{(0,2)\times (1,3)}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{(-1,0)\times (1,3)}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{(0,2)\times (1,3)}2\sqrt{xy}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: The first rectangle contributes 2∫₀^π cos y dy = 0. The second contributes (∫₁² x dx)(∫₀^π sin y dy) = (3/2)·2 = 3. Thus the total is 3.

after.name: Question 19
after.problem:
Evaluate the double integral ${∬}_{R}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A$, where

$$
f(x,y)={\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡y,\, & \text{if}\,-1<x<1,\,0<y<\pi , \\ x\operatorname{sin}⁡y,\, & \text{if}\,1<x<2,\,0<y<\pi ,\end{aligned}
$$

and  $R$ is the domain of $f.$
after.worked_solution:
First, notice that we have $R={R}_{1}\cup {R}_{2}$, where ${R}_{1}=(-1,1)\times (0,\pi )$ and ${R}_{2}=(1,2)\times (0,\pi ).$ So, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A= & ={∬}_{{R}_{1}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{{R}_{2}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{{R}_{1}}\operatorname{cos}⁡y\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{{R}_{2}}x\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,\text{d}A \\  & =(1-(-1)){\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡y\,\text{d}y+({\int }_{1}^{2}x\,\text{d}x)({\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,\text{d}y) \\  & =2[\operatorname{sin}⁡y]_{0}^{\pi }+[\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}]_{1}^{2}\cdot [-\operatorname{cos}⁡y]_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =2(0)+(2-\frac{1}{2})\cdot (-(-1)+1) \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$
